title: Ease of accessibility
description: This latent activates on language describing something as readily obtainable, reachable, or usable without difficulty, as in phrases like 'easily accessible.' It fires on short evaluative or descriptive phrases that emphasize low barriers to access—whether of information, locations, resources, or services. It would not activate on sentences describing difficulty, restriction, or effort required to obtain something, nor on unrelated descriptive content that doesn't concern accessibility or ease of use, such as narrative, emotional, or purely factual statements lacking this accessibility framing.

title: Emotionally-sensitive interpersonal advice framing
description: This latent fires on language from advice/support contexts (e.g., relationship or AITA-style responses) that flags a topic as emotionally sensitive, probes underlying motivations/feelings, or coaches the reader on how to broach or avoid difficult personal disclosures. It activates on exclamatory empathetic framings ('What a sensitive and complex topic!'), motivation-probing questions ('What drives you?', 'What triggers your behavior?'), instructions to share or avoid sharing feelings, and short judgment-toned fragments ('Not entirely.', 'Wrong.') that hedge or evaluate someone's behavior in an emotionally charged interpersonal situation. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, narrative descriptions of events without emotional/interpersonal framing, or advice unrelated to feelings, disclosure, or interpersonal sensitivity.

title: Short exclamatory fragment
description: This latent fires on brief, syntactically incomplete utterances that function as exclamatory or emphatic fragments rather than full grammatical sentences—often a single word, an exclamation with an implied subject, or a noun phrase followed by an exclamation point. These fragments typically convey emotional emphasis, reaction, or commentary on a situation (e.g., acknowledging pressure, tenderness, or agreement) rather than stating propositional content in standard subject-verb-object form. It would not activate on complete, declarative sentences that fully articulate a thought with subject and predicate, nor on neutral factual statements lacking exclamatory punctuation or fragment structure—even if they discuss similar emotional topics like parenting or stress.

title: Employment/hiring statements about occupations
description: This latent activates on sentences that state facts about who employs or hires workers for a particular job or role, often naming the type of employer (e.g., government agencies, private companies) alongside the occupation. It responds to general, factual statements about employment practices or labor market patterns rather than narratives about a specific individual's job experience. It would not activate on sentences merely describing job duties, personal anecdotes about working, or job advertisements phrased as direct calls to apply, since the key pattern is a declarative statement about hiring/employment relationships.

title: Advice to identify and manage something
description: This latent fires on imperative, self-help style phrasing that instructs the reader to become aware of and control some internal state or factor (e.g., 'Learn to recognize and manage your...'). It activates on sentence openings that combine a cognitive verb like 'recognize' or 'identify' with a regulatory verb like 'manage' or 'control', typically directed at the reader via imperative mood and possessive framing ('your'). It would not activate on purely descriptive statements about emotions or behaviors, third-person narration, or advice that lacks this recognize-then-manage instructional structure.
